use the relationship between power, work done (energy transferred) and time taken: power = time taken work done W P = t

primer.text: The same job done faster is a more powerful machine. These lessons define power as the rate of energy transfer, walk the ratings scale from torches to power stations, and practise the power equation in both directions.

modules.title: Power as the rate of doing work
sourceHeadings: Two cars with different power ratings doing the same amount of work
modules.opening: Power measures how quickly energy moves, not how much moves in total. Two machines can deliver identical amounts of energy, yet the more powerful one finishes sooner — that speed of delivery is the whole definition.
keyPoints: Power is work done per unit time, and therefore energy transferred per unit time.
Machines such as car engines transfer energy between stores continuously over time.
Two vehicles can do the same work; the more powerful one completes it in a shorter time.
Two motors lifting the same weight the same height differ in power if one lifts faster.
Power ratings on appliances state the energy transferred each second, from watts to megawatts.

low.restatement: Power is a pace, not a pile: the same sack of energy delivered in half the time means double the power. A torch trickles joules, an oven pours them, a power station floods them.
low.analogy: Two gardeners moving the same pile of bricks: the faster one earns the same wage in half the shift — their hourly rate is their power.
low.examPointer: When comparing machines, hold the energy or work fixed and let the time differ — that is what isolates power in an exam description.

medium.restatement: Power is defined as the rate of energy transfer, equivalently the rate of doing work: identical transfers over different durations carry different powers. Ratings express that rate — a 10 kW oven transfers ten thousand joules every second it runs.
medium.analogy: A tap's flow rate: two tanks can end with the same water, but the wider tap filled in less time — flow rate is to water what power is to energy.
medium.examPointer: Quote power in watts and convert kilowatts and megawatts before any equation work — 1 kW = 1000 W, 1 MW = 1 000 000 W.

modules.title: Calculating power
sourceHeadings: Power, work done and time formula triangle
modules.opening: The power equation connects three everyday quantities: the work done, the time taken and the rate — power itself. A formula triangle handles every rearrangement, whether a question hides the power, the energy or the time.
keyPoints: P = W ÷ t, with power in watts, work done in joules and time in seconds.
Rearranged, the work done equals power multiplied by time, and time equals work done divided by power.
A formula triangle covering P, W or t reproduces each rearrangement of the equation.
Time must enter the equation in seconds for the power to come out in watts.

low.restatement: Divide the joules by the seconds and you have the watts. Hide P on the triangle and W over t appears; hide W and P next to t multiplies; hide t and W over P divides.
low.analogy: A pay cheque: total earned (joules) divided by hours worked (seconds) gives the hourly rate (watts) — and the triangle rearranges for whichever of the three the question hides.
low.examPointer: Convert minutes to seconds before dividing — the classic slip is using 5 instead of 300 for a five-minute appliance.

medium.restatement: The equation P = W/t prices energy transfer per second: W in joules (or newton-metres), t in seconds, P in watts. The triangle encodes W = Pt, P = W/t and t = W/P for the quantity a question withholds.
medium.analogy: A currency converter with three windows: cover the one you need and the other two show whether to multiply or divide.
medium.examPointer: Annotate every value with its unit before substituting — mixed units (minutes, kilojoules) are how power answers go wrong.

glossary.definition: The rate at which energy is transferred or work is done, measured in watts.
The unit of power; one watt is one joule of energy transferred each second.
One thousand watts, the rating unit of many household appliances.

workedExample.prompt: Calculate the work done if an iron of power 2000 W is used for 5 minutes.
steps: List the known values: power P = 2000 W and time t = 5 minutes = 5 × 60 = 300 s.
State the equation: P = W ÷ t.
Rearrange for the work done: W = P × t.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The iron does 600 000 J of work in five minutes.
